periods.analysis: Quick read: Average Customer Service Response Time came in green at 3.3 hours against the <=4 hour target, with no priorValue and delta null because this is our first quarter in the series. The 311 feed is clean for this baseline pull, and Utilities Dispatch used the new PW-CS tagging set for leaks, pressure calls, meter questions, and billing handoffs. That 3.3 is a solid starting point for a fast-growing city like Harborview, especially with summer move-ins adding volume along the East Marina and Bluffview routes. Tiny anomaly worth noting: Friday afternoon meter-box calls closed faster than weekday mornings, likely because Crew 4 was already staged near permit inspections.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the PW-CS tags locked and doing a weekly 311 feed spot-check before the ClearPoint update. Extend the East Marina staging pattern into the fall service map, since it appears to be shaving response time without adding overtime. I’ll keep the baseline note attached so nobody reads the null priorValue as a data miss.

periods.analysis: Q4 stayed green at 3.9 hours, up 0.6 hours from 3.3 in 2024-Q3 but still under the <=4 hour target. The increase lines up with holiday staffing, two atmospheric-river weekends, and a heavier run of after-hours pressure complaints in the Harbor Heights pressure zone. The 311 feed matched the dispatch export after we fixed four duplicate voicemail tickets from the North Pier call group, so the number looks usable. Not panicking here, but 3.9 is close enough to the line that I’m flagging it early 👍.
periods.recommendations: Keep the result green by maintaining the storm-weekend callback script and assigning one backup analyst to reconcile 311 and dispatch duplicates every Monday. Add a watch-item for Harbor Heights pressure-zone calls if they exceed 12 open tickets at noon on any weekday. For Q1, test a pre-triage queue for weather-related calls so operators can separate urgent utility responses from general storm questions faster.

periods.analysis: Q1 improved to 3.7 hours, down 0.2 hours from 3.9 in 2024-Q4, so we stayed green with a little more breathing room under the <=4 hour target. The main driver looks like the January rollout of the 311 quick-disposition buttons for meter resets, low-pressure checks, and service-line owner questions. Dispatch also kept the winter leak calls on Route W-12 grouped by neighborhood, which reduced back-and-forth between crews and the call desk. Useful anomaly: Spanish-language callback tickets closed slightly faster than the overall average after Rosa and Malik started the bilingual callback block.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green trend by making the quick-disposition buttons permanent in the 311 feed and auditing 20 closed tickets per month for correct coding. Extend the bilingual callback block to two afternoons per week through Q2, since it is helping response time and resident clarity. Keep the Route W-12 clustering playbook available for the next cold-snap response.

periods.analysis: Q2 moved to 3.4 hours, down 0.3 hours from 3.7 in 2025-Q1, and the measure remains green against the <=4 hour target. This is the best result since the 2024-Q3 baseline, and it happened while spring permit activity picked up around South Cove and the Transit Village utility tie-ins. The 311 feed shows fewer reopenings after we added the “resolved by field visit” closure note for meter-lid, curb-stop, and hydrant questions. Nice little signal: tickets touched by the morning utility-service huddle averaged under the citywide number, so the huddle is doing real work.
periods.recommendations: Keep the morning utility-service huddle in place and require each supervisor to bring the top five aging 311 tickets before crews roll. Extend the “resolved by field visit” note to billing-transfer tickets so Customer Service can reduce unnecessary reopenings. I’d also keep South Cove permit calls in a separate dashboard slice through the summer, just to catch growth pressure before it shows up in the headline average.

periods.analysis: Q3 edged down again to 3.3 hours, a 0.1 hour improvement from 3.4 in 2025-Q2, keeping us green and matching the original 2024-Q3 baseline value. That’s a good sign because summer demand was not light: irrigation starts, move-in calls near Bayview Landing, and hydrant-flow questions all hit the 311 feed. The “top five aging tickets” huddle seems to be holding, especially for meter access issues assigned to Crews 2 and 5. One anomaly nobody asked for: Saturday web-form tickets are now being acknowledged faster than Tuesday phone tickets, which is backwards but useful.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 3.3 hour performance by keeping Saturday web-form auto-routing active and copying that routing rule to Tuesday phone-intake follow-ups. Extend the aging-ticket huddle to include one Customer Service lead during high-growth weeks at Bayview Landing. Keep checking the 311 feed for channel mix, because the phone-versus-web gap could hide a training need.

periods.analysis: Q4 rose to 3.9 hours, up 0.6 hours from 3.3 in 2025-Q3, but it still finished green under the <=4 hour target. This looks very similar to last Q4: holiday coverage, stormwater-related utility calls, and a batch of low-pressure reports after the Westside valve exercising work. The 311 feed reconciled after we excluded eight vendor test tickets from the IVR upgrade, so I’m comfortable with the posted value. Watch item: 3.9 is green, but it is again sitting right at the edge of yellow territory if one busy week goes sideways.
periods.recommendations: Protect the green status by pre-scheduling a holiday coverage bridge between Customer Service, Utilities Dispatch, and the Westside field supervisor. Keep vendor test tickets tagged as NONPERF in the 311 feed so they do not drift into the performance extract. For the next winter cycle, extend the storm callback script to include low-pressure FAQs tied to valve exercising notices.

periods.analysis: Q1 improved to 3.6 hours, down 0.3 hours from 3.9 in 2025-Q4, so the measure is safely green again. The post-holiday reset worked: the 311 feed shows faster first-touch times after Dispatch shifted one operator from 7:30–9:30 a.m. to catch overnight web forms. Crews also used the Westside valve-work notice list to answer repeat low-pressure questions without creating new field visits. Small anomaly: the Lakefront District had more total tickets than South Cove, but South Cove still had the longer tail, mostly from new-account meter questions.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the 7:30–9:30 a.m. overnight web-form coverage through at least the end of Q2. Extend the Westside notice-list approach to South Cove new-account meter questions and add a one-page script for Customer Service. I’ll keep a separate South Cove tail report attached so the average does not hide that localized drag.

periods.analysis: June response time closed at 3.5 hours against a 4.0-hour target, the fourth consecutive month inside target and the best result of the fiscal year to date. The improvement traces primarily to the call-back triage change introduced in March, which routes non-emergency water pressure and billing inquiries to the online request form and frees dispatch capacity for field-response calls. Volume was seasonally elevated — irrigation-season pressure complaints typically peak in June — so holding 3.5 hours through that peak indicates the gain is structural rather than a quiet-month artifact.
periods.recommendations: Hold the current staffing pattern through the remainder of irrigation season rather than reallocating dispatch coverage. Recommend tightening the internal working target to 3.5 hours for FY27 planning while leaving the published target at 4.0, so the buffer absorbs storm-event surges. Ask IT to segment the metric by request channel next quarter — phone versus online — to confirm the online form is absorbing volume rather than deferring it.

periods.analysis: Average first response held at 3.9 hours against a 4.0-hour target. Response time absorbed the Maple St incident volume better than closure did — the after-hours dispatch rotation added in Q1-26 kept intake within target even at peak load on 7/28–7/31, when daily request volume ran 4.3x normal.
periods.recommendations: Keep the after-hours rotation funded through Q4-26. It is the main reason response time stayed green while SLA closure slipped, and it is the cheaper of the two levers available for the winter main-break season.
